narrative: This release carries the dataset's two largest technical events at once. Active codes rose +16,046 (to 853,835), but alongside the additions sit 75,232 encoding repairs and a staggering 94,747 municipality (CSD) reassignments — the bulk of all such changes in the entire series.

The encoding wave is the mojibake cleanup: accented French names stored as garbled bytes were normalised. Montréal (19,808), Québec (18,772), Trois-Rivières (5,857) and Lévis (5,395) alone account for over 49,000. No place was renamed; the feed's character encoding was repaired.

The CSD reassignments run in parallel and land in the same provinces: Quebec (78,406) and New Brunswick (14,739). This is a wholesale recode of the municipality field, not physical boundary change — postal codes re-aligned to updated Census Subdivision identifiers across francophone Canada.

Genuine city renames stay modest (1,163). The largest, Victoria → Langford (797, BC), is the mirror image of Feb 2026's Langford → Victoria — the same Greater Victoria boundary reclassified back and forth between releases, a sign the underlying designation is unsettled.

csd_changed: 94,747 reassignments — about 72% of every CSD change in the series — concentrated in Quebec and New Brunswick. This is an administrative recode: postal codes remapped to revised Census Subdivision identifiers en masse, riding along with the same francophone-name cleanup that drove the encoding fixes.
encoding: The single largest mojibake repair in the dataset. Because the biggest cities carry the most codes, Montréal, Québec, Trois-Rivières and Lévis alone are ~49,000 of the 75,232 — a pure encoding artefact, quarantined from every real total.
boundary: Victoria → Langford (797) reverses in a later release (Langford → Victoria). When the same metro boundary flips direction between snapshots, it usually means the source is toggling between two valid designations rather than a real annexation each cycle.
